data.title: NICE backs first oral HAE attack treatment
data.description:
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has issued final draft guidance recommending sebetralstat as an oral, on-demand treatment option for hereditary angioedema (HAE) attacks in adults and adolescents aged 12 years and older on the NHS in England and Wales.

KalVista Pharmaceuticals welcomed the recommendation, which covers use of the treatment within its marketing authorisation. Sebetralstat is designed for the on-demand treatment of HAE attacks and works by blocking plasma kallikrein, a protein that plays a key role in the swelling associated with the condition.

HAE is a rare genetic disorder that causes unpredictable attacks of tissue swelling in different parts of the body. Attacks can be painful and, depending on their location, potentially life-threatening.

The condition is estimated to affect between 1,000 and 1,500 people across the UK.

The NICE recommendation was informed by findings from the phase 3 KONFIDENT clinical trial, which was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, three-way cross-over study published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

Across the study, 110 patients treated a total of 264 HAE attacks. Of these, 87 attacks were treated with sebetralstat 300 mg and 84 with placebo.

Results showed a statistically significant faster time to the beginning of symptom relief with sebetralstat 300 mg compared with placebo.

The median time to the beginning of symptom relief was 1.61 hours with sebetralstat 300 mg, compared with 6.72 hours for placebo.

Clinical studies used for registration have involved treatment of 1,945 HAE attacks with sebetralstat.

According to the company, the most common adverse reaction reported in HAE patients treated with sebetralstat was headache, affecting 9.2% of patients. Reported headaches were generally mild to moderate in severity, non-serious and resolved without further intervention.

Treatment guidelines recommend that HAE attacks are treated as early as possible to help prevent progression of swelling and reduce the time taken for attacks to resolve.

data.title: GSK reports positive phase 3 EGPA trial results
data.description:
GSK has reported positive headline results from its phase 3 OCEAN trial evaluating Exdensur (depemokimab) in patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA).

The non-inferiority study compared twice-yearly depemokimab with monthly mepolizumab in patients receiving standard of care treatment.

According to GSK, the trial met its primary endpoint, demonstrating that depemokimab was non-inferior to mepolizumab in achieving disease remission, which is considered a key treatment goal in EGPA.

The company also reported that the overall incidence and severity of adverse events were similar between treatment groups. Safety findings were consistent with the established profile of depemokimab.

EGPA is a chronic inflammatory disease involving inflammation of small and medium blood vessels. The condition can lead to organ damage and may become life-threatening if not treated appropriately.

Patients are commonly treated with high-dose oral corticosteroids and immunosuppressants. However, GSK noted that these approaches are often insufficient to maintain disease control, leaving patients at risk of relapse and treatment-related complications.

The findings support depemokimab’s potential to become the first ultra-long-acting treatment option for EGPA, requiring dosing only twice a year.

Dr Kaivan Khavandi, SVP, global head of respiratory, immunology & inflammation R&D at GSK, said: “These data reinforce depemokimab’s ultra-long-acting profile, showing that it could help patients achieve disease remission with twice-yearly dosing, reducing the need for corticosteroids and other immunosuppressive therapies.

We look forward to sharing the results with regulators to help further evolve the standard of care for people living with EGPA.”

Full results from the OCEAN study will be submitted for presentation at a future scientific congress and publication in a peer-reviewed journal.

GSK said the data will also support regulatory submissions to health authorities worldwide, with filings planned during the first half of 2027.

Depemokimab is not currently approved for the treatment of EGPA. The medicine is approved in several markets for severe asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps.

data.title: Simcere and Almirall report phase 2 study success
data.description:
Simcere and Almirall have announced positive Week 16 results from a phase 2 study of IL-2mu-Fc (SIM0278/LAD603) in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, with the trial meeting its primary endpoint and one of two key secondary endpoints.

The randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study enrolled 184 adult patients and evaluated the efficacy, safety and pharmacokinetics of three subcutaneous doses of SIM0278 compared with placebo.

According to the companies, two doses of SIM0278 delivered statistically significant improvements from baseline in Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) scores at Week 16 compared with placebo.

Statistically significant improvements were also reported in the proportion of patients achieving clear or almost clear skin, measured by Investigator’s Global Assessment (IGA 0/1). The second key secondary endpoint, EASI-75, showed numerical improvement.

One treatment dose also led to a statistically significant increase in the proportion of patients achieving EASI-90 compared with placebo at Week 16.

The companies said the treatment demonstrated an acceptable safety and tolerability profile, with most treatment-emergent adverse events reported as mild or moderate in intensity.

Dr Karl Ziegelbauer, chief scientific officer at Almirall, said: “These Week 16 results are an encouraging step in our focus on finding new treatment options for people living with atopic dermatitis, and a milestone in our collaboration with Simcere.

We look forward to evaluating the 52 Weeks data investigating maintenance from this study, while also advancing our ongoing study of IL-2mu-Fc in alopecia areata.”

Dr Aik Goh, chief medical officer of Simcere, explained: “We are pleased to see SIM0278 achieve proof of concept in patients with atopic dermatitis. Through receptor-affinity engineering, the molecule selectively directs IL-2 signaling toward regulatory T cells—a first-in-class approach to immune rebalancing.”

He added: “Together with our partner, we will accelerate its global clinical development to bring this potential treatment option to patients as soon as possible.”

The study remains ongoing and will continue through Week 52, with detailed findings expected to be presented at a future scientific congress. Under a licensing agreement signed in 2022, Almirall holds exclusive development and commercialisation rights for SIM0278 outside Greater China, while Simcere retains those rights within the region.

data.title: First patient enters NUZ-001 extension study
data.description:
The first participant in Regimen I of Neurizon Therapeutics’ phase 2/3 HEALEY ALS Platform Trial has completed the 36-week randomised controlled trial phase and moved into the active treatment extension (ATE).

The milestone allows eligible participants to continue receiving investigational treatment with NUZ-001 under the trial protocol. Regimen I is fully enrolled, with 250 participants recruited across 78 US clinical sites.

The ATE is designed to generate additional long-term safety, tolerability, functional and biomarker data to support the continuing development of NUZ-001. Participants will undergo ongoing clinical assessments, including measures of functional decline, respiratory function and quality of life.

Blood and urine biomarker testing, including neurofilament light chain (NfL), will also continue throughout the extension period. Treatment assignments will remain blinded during the extension.

The development follows recent written feedback from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which indicated that positive results from the HEALEY ALS Platform Trial may support a traditional approval pathway and that Regimen I could serve as a single registrational study for NUZ-001, subject to regulatory requirements being met.

Chief executive officer Dr Chris Bremer said: “The first participant entering the Active Treatment Extension is an important milestone for Regimen I and reflects the continued progress of our clinical development program.

“For people living with ALS, a progressive disease with limited treatment options, advancing research into potential new therapies is critically important.”

Dr Bremer added: “The extension provides an opportunity to build our understanding of NUZ-001 through longer-term treatment exposure and clinical observations, complementing the randomised evaluation at the heart of the trial.

“With all 250 participants enrolled, our focus remains on rigorous trial execution and the anticipated topline readout in late Q2 CY2027, while continuing to build the clinical evidence needed to inform the next stages of NUZ-001 development.”

Merit Cudkowicz, executive director of the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute and director of the Healey & AMG Center for ALS, explained: “After enrolling 250 participants in 5 months, we are excited to now have taken this next step in Regimen I of the HEALEY ALS Platform Trial.

“We sincerely thank the study teams, research partners, and participants and their families for their dedication to this trial and helping to advance ALS research.”

data.title: Updated data bolster pancreatic cancer programme
data.description:
Revolution Medicines has reported updated phase 1/2 data showing that its RASONQUE (daraxonrasib) combination regimen continued to deliver deep and durable responses in patients with first-line metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC).

The latest findings from the RMC-GI-102 study were presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR (ENA) Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain. Results support the ongoing phase 3 RASolute 303 trial in treatment-naïve metastatic pancreatic cancer.

As of 28 September 2026, 61 patients had received RASONQUE plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel (GnP) in the first-line metastatic PDAC cohort, with a median follow-up of 18.3 months.

The updated analysis showed a confirmed objective response rate of 60.7%, including complete responses in 8.2% of patients. The disease control rate was 90.2%, while the median duration of response was 11.1 months.

Median progression-free survival reached 12.8 months and the estimated 12-month overall survival rate was 76.6%. The safety profile was reported to be consistent with previous observations for both RASONQUE and GnP.

Dr Wungki Park, medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and investigator for the study, said: “With longer follow-up and a larger patient population, we are seeing a notable combination of high response rates, including deep complete responses, and durable disease control, with median progression-free survival exceeding one year.”

He added: “The emerging survival signal is meaningful and is estimated at 76.6% for patients to be alive at one year. Taken together, these findings provide a compelling rationale to further evaluate daraxonrasib as a potential first-line treatment option.”

The programme recently received FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation for RASONQUE plus GnP in this setting.

Dr Alan Sandler, chief development officer of Revolution Medicines, explained: “People with treatment-naïve metastatic pancreatic cancer urgently need more effective treatment options, given the limited clinical benefit of current chemotherapy regimens.”

He added: “The durability of treatment shown with these updated phase 1/2 results is particularly encouraging and supports the ongoing phase 3 RASolute 303 trial.”

data.title: SRD Search launches on VIDAL with first pharmaceutical company – Pfizer
data.description:
Datapharm, the company behind emc, the UK’s trusted source of regulatory-approved medicines information, has announced the launch of its SRD Search functionality on VIDAL in France.

Pfizer is the first manufacturer to make its Scientific Response Documents (SRDs) available to French healthcare professionals (HCPs) through the service. Since going live in August 2026, Pfizer has published 373 French SRDs covering nine of its brands.

France is the third market for SRD Search, following the UK on emc and Germany on Rote Liste. Fourteen pharmaceutical companies currently use the service across the three markets, with take-up continuing to grow.

Search data from the UK and Germany has already shown that HCP behaviour differs by market. In Germany, nine in ten searches are a single word and more than half are typed in English rather than German. In both markets, a significant share of searches happens outside the hours a Medical Information service is typically staffed.

The launch on VIDAL marks the start of building the same level of insight for France. Participating manufacturers receive analytics reports showing what French HCPs search for, when they search and which questions go unanswered, helping them refine their SRD content for the French market.

Rob Morgan, Chief Executive Officer, Datapharm, said: “Healthcare professionals need answers they can trust, yet increasingly the first answer they see comes from a tool that cannot distinguish a verified response from an invented one. Manufacturers have already done the hard work of writing and reviewing these documents. SRD Search puts that trusted content where French HCPs already look, at any hour. Launching on VIDAL with Pfizer is an important step in expanding access to trusted medicine information across Europe, and the beginning of understanding how French HCPs search.”

Aqid Iqbal, Europe and Canada Medical Information Operations Manager, Pfizer, said: “Expanding access to Pfizer Medical Information through VIDAL is an important step in our Medical Information strategy of easing access and expanding reach. We are proud that Pfizer is the first manufacturer to make Scientific Response Documents available through this new service on VIDAL. By making trusted Pfizer Scientific Response Documents available through a resource healthcare professionals in France already use, we are enabling greater self-service access to medical information, where and when it is needed. This collaboration builds on our work to bring trusted scientific information closer to healthcare professionals through established digital channels, helping ensure that the science behind our breakthroughs is supported by accessible medical information for those caring for patients.”

Ferran Portella, Managing Director of VIDAL Group’s Medical Knowledge Solutions division, said: “VIDAL’s role is to provide French healthcare professionals with accurate and reliable information on medicines. SRD Search extends what they can find on vidal.fr with approved, in-depth responses from manufacturers, accessible 24/7 whenever they need to make a prescription decision. We are pleased to welcome Pfizer as the first manufacturer on the service.”

Issued by Datapharm Ltd, Cassini Court, Randalls Way, Leatherhead KT22 7TW, on 16 November 2026

data.title: Accelerating patient care
data.description:
A laboratory breakthrough can attract headlines long before a treatment reaches patients. For innovative life sciences companies, progress depends on the evidence behind each discovery.

Recent breakthroughs in life sciences equipment offer new ways to examine that evidence. Their practical value rests on how well they help researchers evaluate discoveries and support clinical development.

The scale and attrition behind every scientific breakthrough

The global drug development pipeline is approaching 22,940 candidates in 2026, about four times its size in 2001. Some 7,057 companies have active pipelines, with immunological anticancer products accounting for 4,852 pipeline candidates.

In 2024, Merck & Co. reportedly invested heavily in research and development. Pfizer spent $10.822 billion in 2024 alone.

For drugs entering phase 2 with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), just one in three advances to phase 3. This puts advancement beyond phase 3 at approximately 33%.

Clinical trials must establish treatment benefit, so laboratory capabilities address only part of the development pathway.

Precision starting materials shape every downstream result

Genomics and metabolomics workflows require researchers to isolate the material they intend to analyse. Danaher, a life sciences technology provider, offers laser microdissection for sample collection to address this preparation step prior to molecular testing.

According to the company, the systems can “collect pure starting materials for analysis under visual supervision”. During dissection, the laser moves while the specimen remains stationary and gravity collects the isolated material.

Metabolite data shaping the future of diagnostics

Liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-MS) can generate data sets that stretch laboratory review capacity. Danaher Corporation identifies manual preparation and study comparisons as potential bottlenecks when analytical workloads grow.

Danaher notes that “labs need to scale insight and throughput without scaling manual effort or variability”. Its metabolite solutions page describes the SCIEX ZenoTOF 8600 system as offering up to 10x greater sensitivity for biomarker discovery and validation.

It also reports improvements exceeding 80% in biotherapeutic sample recovery and consistency with Biozen LC columns.

Scaling image analysis without losing rigour

Danaher offers microscope image analysis software for image visualisation and interpretation across two to five dimensions. Its platform uses artificial intelligence (AI) as a core architectural feature and supports instruments ranging from confocal to light-sheet microscopes.

The company states that the software analyses images in minutes, including complex imaging data sets. Laboratories should assess performance against their own imaging tasks before setting throughput expectations or adopting the software within established review procedures.

Where research investment can support the next leap

Research budgets should reflect the bottleneck each team needs to address. Before committing funds to another instrument, a laboratory expanding LC-MS capacity can assess whether its existing sample preparation and review processes can accommodate the additional output.

Danaher’s metabolite analysis workflow connects preparation with measurement and scalable data analysis. Teams can use that sequence to assess where additional resources would support the next development decision, whether through more consistent preparation or greater capacity to compare results across studies.

Frequently asked questions about taking discoveries from bench to bedside

Equipment capabilities address specific research tasks along the development pathway. Their relevance depends on the evidence each team needs to generate and evaluate.

What is the latest technology in life sciences research tools?

Precision laser microdissection supports sample isolation, while high-resolution LC-MS enables detailed molecular measurement. AI image analysis software adds computational tools for examining microscopy data sets.

What are the most significant breakthroughs in life sciences equipment recently?

The SCIEX ZenoTOF 8600 is an example of a system that offers increased sensitivity for biomarker discovery and validation. In microscopy, Danaher’s software combines an AI-centred architecture with visualisation and analysis across multiple dimensions.

Which life sciences companies invest the most in R&D?

Pharmaceutical research has a substantial development pipeline, with oncology accounting for a particularly large share of activity. Immunological anticancer products are the largest therapeutic category by number of pipeline candidates.

Companies such as Merck & Co. and Pfizer are among the leading pharmaceutical R&D spenders in 2024.

Closing the distance between discovery and care

Moving a discovery towards patient care takes careful testing at every stage. Researchers need suitable samples and reliable analysis to decide which findings warrant further development.

The future of diagnostics will depend on providing teams with the tools and sustained funding to validate promising results.

data.title: Bedside manners
data.description:
Four lessons from electronic renewals that matter as AI enters patient support

Consider a patient receiving a long-term therapy through a drug manufacturer’s assistance programme. As renewal approaches, their insurance details have changed, or their income status has changed. The patient can complete an online form, but the prescriber must confirm another part of the application. Then a secure link expires. The problem is no longer how quickly software processes a form; it is whether someone can recover the case without making both parties begin again.

Patient assistance automation is often evaluated by how many manual steps it removes. That is a useful measure, but an incomplete one. The more revealing test is what happens when a renewal does not follow the expected path: who is alerted, what information travels with the exception and how quickly an accountable person can act.

I worked on the technology integration for an electronic patient assistance programme (ePAP) enrolment and renewal initiative at a US rare-disease company in 2023. The programme design introduced separate digital application paths for patients and prescribers, linked the portal to an existing patient-services environment and supported renewal communications at scale.

It was conventional workflow automation, not AI. Yet it exposed four design decisions that matter even more as AI enters patient support.

1. Design around the people who complete the application

A renewal is not one document completed by one person. Patients, carers, prescribers and support staff have different responsibilities, information and permissions. Moving a paper form online does little if the same information still has to be repeatedly collected or checked by the wrong participant.

Our integration design specified distinct patient and prescriber experiences, with secure links and additional verification for prescribers. It also defined how existing patient details could be retrieved to support the online process. The broader lesson is to divide the workflow according to who can reliably supply or attest to each piece of information. Automation should reduce unnecessary repetition without blurring responsibility for clinical or eligibility-related information.

2. Engineer the failure path before celebrating the happy path

The most instructive design discussions concerned exceptions. What happens if a link expires? If verification fails repeatedly? If an email address is missing or needs updating? The workflow we designed specified status notifications, ways to request replacement links and escalation paths involving support staff. These were not peripheral error messages. They were part of the service.

The same principle applies when an AI tool reads a document, suggests missing information or proposes the next action. A low-confidence extraction or a conflicting answer should not disappear into a dashboard. It needs an explicit handover: the reason for referral, the supporting information, the responsible team and a way to see whether the case was resolved. The system should be designed around recoverability, not an assumption that every transaction will succeed.

3. Return completed information to the operational record

A digital portal can provide an excellent experience while leaving case managers with another silo. Our integration design specified the return of application information to the patient-services environment, including relevant patient, prescriber and consent information and supporting materials. The aim was to keep the operational record usable after the online interaction ended.

For leaders evaluating AI, that is a more demanding requirement than a successful demonstration. Where will a proposed answer, a validated field or an unresolved exception appear? Can staff identify its origin and correct it without re-entering everything? If the output is disconnected from the record people rely on, automation has merely relocated administrative work.

4. Keep accountability separate from automation

Electronic applications can collect information and apply predefined validation steps. They should not be mistaken for a complete, independently accountable determination of a patient’s eligibility. Where rules are ambiguous, information conflicts or supporting documents are incomplete, people need a clear path to review the case and explain what happens next.

That principle has a regulatory dimension, although obligations differ by programme and country. UK rules on solely automated significant decisions include safeguards such as the ability to obtain human intervention and contest a decision. In the EU, certain direct interactions with AI systems trigger transparency obligations. Neither framework should be casually applied to a US assistance programme; both reinforce why the boundary between automated processing and consequential decisions deserves deliberate design.

My subsequent review of AI in healthcare CRM examined opportunities from automation alongside the need for privacy, transparency and responsible implementation. The practical question I would bring to any new tool is simpler: when it cannot complete a task safely, can it transfer the work to a person with enough context to act?

Measure the handover, not just the throughput

A 2026 Guidehouse survey reported a 23-point decline in pharmaceutical leaders using third-party hub services, reflecting a shift towards more internal and hybrid patient-support models. Whether services are delivered by a manufacturer, a partner or both, someone must own the unresolved case. The technology cannot settle that accountability on its own.

I would therefore track completion time, and also expired-link recovery, cases awaiting review, information that must be requested again and the time between an exception and a human response. These are recommended measures, not documented outcomes from the 2023 initiative. They test the quality of the experience when automation meets its limits.

Return to the patient facing renewal. Success is not simply receiving a faster online form. It is completing the right steps once, knowing what remains outstanding and having a real route forward when something goes wrong. That is the standard that patient assistance automation, and any AI layered on top of it, should be built to meet.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jaymin Sutarwala is Associate Director, CRM Strategy & Operations at United Therapeutics. His work spans patient-services technology, healthcare CRM integrations and pharmaceutical workflow automation

data.title: ViiV wins CHMP backing for paediatric HIV drugs
data.description:
ViiV Healthcare has received positive opinions from the European Medicines Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) recommending expanded use of Tivicay and Dovato in younger children living with HIV across the EU.

The recommendations are aimed at addressing ongoing treatment gaps in paediatric HIV care. According to ViiV, only 55% of children living with HIV globally received antiretroviral therapy in 2024, while around half of untreated infants with HIV die before reaching two years of age.

The CHMP recommended extending the indication for Tivicay (dolutegravir) dispersible tablets for use in HIV-infected adults, adolescents, children and term neonates from birth weighing at least 2kg when used with other antiretroviral medicines.

If approved, ViiV said Tivicay would become the first second-generation integrase inhibitor available in the EU for eligible newborns.

The committee also recommended approval of a new dispersible tablet formulation of Dovato (dolutegravir/lamivudine) for children aged at least three months and weighing between 6kg and less than 25kg. An extension to the existing film-coated tablet indication for children weighing at least 20kg was also recommended.

If approved, Dovato could become the first single-tablet, two-drug treatment option for eligible younger children living with HIV in the EU.

Jean van Wyk, Chief Medical Officer at ViiV Healthcare, said: “Children living with HIV require lifelong care, making continued innovation essential. If approved, Tivicay would become the first second-generation integrase inhibitor to offer eligible newborns dolutegravir-based treatment, while Dovato would bring the first single tablet, two-drug regimen option to eligible younger children.”

He added: “These positive CHMP opinions mark an important step towards expanding age-appropriate, INSTI-based treatment options for children and advancing our goal of offering greater choice in HIV care, so more people living with HIV can benefit from innovative treatment options at every stage of life.”

The applications were supported by data from the IMPAACT 2023, Penta-21 and DANCE studies. European Commission decisions are expected in the first quarter of 2027.

data.title: First patient dosed in Tiprelestat PAH study
data.description:
The first patient has been dosed in a phase 2 clinical study evaluating Tiprelestat as a potential treatment for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), according to tiakis Biotech AG.

The Athena study is being conducted by Stanford University under the leadership of Dr Roham Zamanian, Dr Marlene Rabinovitch and Dr Cathie Spino. The trial is sponsored through a National Institutes of Health grant awarded to Stanford University in 2025.

Tiprelestat is a biological neutrophil elastase inhibitor designed to enhance BMPR2 signalling. The investigational treatment is being developed as a potentially disease-modifying therapy for PAH.

Dr Roham Zamanian, Director of the Adult Pulmonary Hypertension Service at the Vera Moulton Wall Center for Pulmonary Vascular Disease at Stanford University, said: “We are very excited by the prospect of bringing Tiprelestat to the PAH clinic and assessing its disease-modifying potential in this patient population with a persistently high unmet medical need.”

According to the company, preclinical studies have shown the potential to address underlying inflammation and reverse vascular remodelling associated with the disease.

tiakis said Tiprelestat has so far demonstrated an excellent safety profile across five clinical trials involving more than 100 individuals.

PAH is a rare disease characterised by high blood pressure in the arteries that supply the lungs. The company said total prevalence across the seven major global markets was estimated at around 112,700 cases in 2024, with numbers projected to increase through 2034.

The United States accounts for around 45% of diagnosed PAH cases, according to the company.

Tiprelestat has received Orphan Designation in both Europe and the United States.

Martin Voss, chief executive officer of tiakis Biotech AG, explained: “Based on the very encouraging results from the previous clinical trials and preclinical disease models of PAH, we are pleased to advance Tiprelestat into this Athena trial in collaboration with Stanford University.”

The company described Tiprelestat as a first- and best-in-class therapeutic candidate with potential to modify the course of disease rather than solely manage symptoms.
